status_note: Weights and anchors below are a mine and Claude's placeholder. The methodology requires that weights be set by clinical advisory input and statistical analysis of which markers predict resource intensity, not by assertion. Until that work is done, no index computed with this pack should be published.
scope_note: This pack is the instrument for the whole surgical encounter class, not a gynaecology-specific one: it scores the urology, general surgery and orthopaedics comparator cohort with the same markers and weights it scores the study cohort with, so every marker must be reachable in every specialty (no specialty-only marker), though a marker's lexicon may be specialty-tagged internally to recognise how each specialty phrases the same finding.
normalisation_note: Each marker is normalised against fixed anchors published in this file, never against percentiles of the observed cohort. An empirically normalised score changes every time an encounter is added, which would make a published value non-comparable with itself a month later. Fixed anchors cost some dynamic range and buy stability.
lanes_note: Structured markers carry 0.74 of the weight and narrative rules 0.26. Where both lanes offer the same marker the structured value wins, because a score that preferred narrative would measure how thoroughly a surgeon writes rather than how hard the case was.

markers.note: Incision to close, not in-room to out-of-room. Turnover and positioning are real work but they are not the surgeon's operative effort, and in-room time is the more easily gamed of the two. The note usually restates the time; OpTime wins where both exist.
ASA physical status. Published ordinal instrument, assigned pre-operatively by anaesthesia, independent of the surgeon and of billing.
Count of distinct specialties among operating surgeons. A colorectal team in a gynaecological case is the clearest structured signal that the case exceeded what the code contemplates.
Discrete field where the OR record carries one, the note's own statement where it does not.
Distinct CPT codes on the operative log. Counted from documentation, not from what was submitted, so an uncoded procedure still raises complexity.

Distinct structures involved beyond the primary operative field. Read from the findings and the operative description only: an organ named under INDICATION is why the patient is in theatre, not work performed today.

patterns.regex: \b(?:rectosigmoid|recto-sigmoid|sigmoid colon|large bowel|small bowel|bowel wall|rectal wall|rectovaginal septum)\b

markers.note: Crude ordinal from explicit phrasing: dense 3, moderate 2, filmy 1. The methodology reserves the severity a rule cannot reach -- a note that never uses the word -- for the generative enrichment lane. This reads only what is written.
Events that occurred during the case. Distinct kinds, not occurrences: two serosal tears are one kind of event.

procedures.note: Adhesiolysis is CPT 58660, a separate-procedure code: NCCI bundles it into any other laparoscopic gynaecologic procedure done in the same session, so it is billable on its own only when nothing else is done. Documenting it without submitting 58660 alongside one of our other study codes is a mismatch against whichever of those was billed, not a missed charge, because the work was already paid for as part of that code.

Freeing the ureter to expose a pelvic field has no CPT code of its own in our benign-gynaecologic code set; it is understood as part of the exposure for whatever procedure it enabled, not a billable step in its own right. No candidate exists to check the claim against, so a documented mention only ever reports as no_code.

An incidental serosal tear repaired primarily during the same operative session is intraoperative housekeeping, not a separately reportable procedure: there is no CPT code for repairing an injury the index procedure itself caused. No candidate exists to check the claim against.

A genuine conversion to an open approach changes which CPT is billed entirely, from the laparoscopic code to its open equivalent, and that recoding decision belongs to the surgeon and coder, not to this cross-check. We flag only that a conversion was documented, for review; we do not guess at what the open code should have been.
